q: The total assets of an enterprise are Rs 28,00,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 4,00,000. Its net sales are Rs 72,00,000. Its capital employed turnover ratio (net sales divided by total assets minus current liabilities) is:

options.A: 2.57 times
options.B: 3.00 times
options.C: 18.00 times
options.D: 2.40 times

e: Capital employed = total assets - current liabilities = 28,00,000 - 4,00,000 = Rs 24,00,000. Capital employed turnover = 72,00,000 / 24,00,000 = 3.00 times.

q: An enterprise has an equity multiplier (total assets divided by equity shareholders' funds) of 2.5. This means that:

options.A: Its equity shareholders earn a return of 250% on their funds
options.B: Its total assets are two and a half times its equity funds, the balance having been financed by outside liabilities
options.C: Its long-term debt is two and a half times its equity funds
options.D: Its sales are two and a half times its total assets

e: An equity multiplier of 2.5 means total assets are 2.5 times equity shareholders' funds; the balance of the assets has been financed by outside liabilities, showing the degree of leverage.

q: The interest coverage ratio tests only the payment of interest on debt. The debt service coverage ratio is a more complete test of debt servicing because it additionally reckons with:

options.A: The market price of the shares of the enterprise
options.B: The depreciation charged during the year
options.C: The tax rate applicable to the enterprise
options.D: The scheduled repayment of the principal of the debt

e: Interest coverage tests only interest payment, whereas debt service coverage additionally reckons with scheduled repayment of the principal of the debt, making it a more complete test of debt servicing.

q: The gross profit ratio of an enterprise falls in a year in which its sales have actually increased. The most likely explanation is that:

options.A: Its selling and distribution expenses have risen
options.B: Its cost of goods sold has risen proportionately more than its sales, or its selling prices have been cut
options.C: Its interest charges have risen during the year
options.D: Its closing stock has been valued on a different basis by the auditor

e: Gross profit depends on sales and cost of goods sold only. If sales rose but the gross profit ratio fell, cost of goods sold must have risen proportionately more than sales, or selling prices were cut.

q: A comparison of the ratios of an enterprise over a series of years will be dependable only if:

options.A: The enterprise has earned a profit in every one of those years
options.B: The same accounting policies have been followed consistently, or the figures have been adjusted for any change in them
options.C: The sales of the enterprise have increased in every year
options.D: The ratios are compared with the ratios of other enterprises

e: Ratio comparisons over a series of years are dependable only if the same accounting policies were followed consistently, or figures are adjusted for any change, otherwise trends reflect policy changes, not performance.

q: In a factory, departmental managers who comfortably exceed their budget targets in one year find that the management simply raises their targets for the next year in proportion to the achievement. The managers therefore learn to hold back their performance and not exceed the targets by too much. This behavioural effect of budgeting is known as:

options.A: The halo effect
options.B: The ratchet effect, under which current achievement becomes the base for higher future targets and so discourages managers from revealing their full potential
options.C: The Hawthorne effect
options.D: The anchoring effect

e: The ratchet effect arises when current achievement becomes the base for higher future targets, so managers who exceed targets learn to hold back performance and not reveal their full potential.

q: Under the competitive-parity method of fixing the advertising budget, the amount to be spent on advertising is determined by:

options.A: Taking a fixed percentage of the sales of the previous year
options.B: Estimating the cost of the tasks needed to achieve the advertising objectives
options.C: Spending broadly in line with what the competitors are spending, so that the enterprise's share of the total advertising voice in the market roughly matches its share of the market
options.D: Spending whatever funds remain after all the other budgets have been provided for

e: Under competitive-parity, the advertising budget is set broadly in line with competitors' spending, so the enterprise's share of advertising voice in the market roughly matches its share of the market.

q: Under the jury of executive opinion method of forecasting sales for the sales budget, the sales forecast is arrived at by:

options.A: Pooling the considered opinions of the senior executives of the enterprise, drawn from sales, production, finance and other functions, and combining them through discussion into a single agreed forecast
options.B: Applying a statistical trend line to the sales of the past ten years without consulting anyone
options.C: Adding up the estimates sent in by the individual salesmen of their own territories without any review
options.D: Adopting the growth rate forecast by the Government for the economy as a whole

e: The jury of executive opinion method pools the considered opinions of senior executives from sales, production, finance and other functions and combines them through discussion into a single agreed sales forecast.

q: In the classification of styles of budgetary evaluation associated with Hopwood, a 'budget-constrained' style of evaluating a subordinate manager means that:

options.A: The superior ignores the budget figures altogether while evaluating the manager
options.B: The superior evaluates the manager only on the long-term growth of the enterprise
options.C: The superior uses the budget figures flexibly, together with many other considerations
options.D: The superior judges the manager primarily by his ability to meet the budget targets in the short run, a style which tends to create job tension and may induce the manipulation of figures and short-term actions harmful in the long run

e: In Hopwood's budget-constrained style, the superior judges the manager primarily by ability to meet budget targets in the short run, a style that tends to create job tension and may induce manipulation of figures and harmful short-term actions.

q: The correct distinction between budgetary slack and a contingency allowance in a budget is that:

options.A: Slack is a deliberate and undisclosed padding built into the estimates by understating revenues or overstating costs so that the targets become easy to achieve, whereas a contingency allowance is a separate provision openly shown in the budget for genuinely unforeseen items, to be used only with proper approval
options.B: Slack is openly shown in the budget, whereas a contingency allowance is always concealed
options.C: Both the terms mean exactly the same thing and are interchangeable
options.D: A contingency allowance is provided only in the cash budget, whereas slack can occur only in the production budget

e: Budgetary slack is deliberate, undisclosed padding - revenues understated or costs overstated to make targets easy. A contingency allowance is a separate provision openly shown for genuinely unforeseen items, used only with proper approval.

q: In the budgetary control report prepared for a responsibility centre, the sound practice in regard to costs that the manager of the centre cannot control is to:

options.A: Omit all mention of such costs from every report of the enterprise
options.B: Charge such costs to the manager and judge his performance by them in the same way as by controllable costs
options.C: Show such costs separately from the controllable items, the manager being judged on the items he can control, while the non-controllable items are reported for information so that the total cost of the centre remains visible
options.D: Transfer such costs to the sales department in every case

e: In a responsibility centre report, non-controllable costs are shown separately from controllable items: the manager is judged on items he can control, while non-controllable items are reported for information so total centre cost remains visible.

q: The correct distinction between capital budgeting and the capital expenditure budget of an enterprise is that:

options.A: The two terms mean exactly the same thing
options.B: Capital budgeting is the process of appraising and selecting the long-term investment proposals of the enterprise, whereas the capital expenditure budget is the statement, forming a part of the master budget, of the capital outlays planned to be made during the budget period on the proposals so selected
options.C: Capital budgeting deals only with the repairs of plant, whereas the capital expenditure budget deals with new plant
options.D: The capital expenditure budget is prepared by the Government, whereas capital budgeting is done by private enterprises only

e: Capital budgeting is the process of appraising and selecting long-term investment proposals; the capital expenditure budget is the statement in the master budget of the capital outlays planned during the budget period on the proposals so selected.

q: For a large capital project which will take several years to complete, the practice of preparing a separate project budget, in addition to the annual budgets of the enterprise, serves the purpose that:

options.A: The project is exempted from budgetary control after the first year
options.B: Only the expenditure of the first year of the project is ever controlled
options.C: The annual budgets need not provide anything at all for the project
options.D: A budget covering the total estimated cost and the whole life of the project is fixed when the project is sanctioned, the annual budgets providing only the slice relating to each year, so that control can be exercised against the total project cost as well as against each year's allotment

e: A separate project budget fixes the total estimated cost for the whole life of a multi-year project at sanction, while annual budgets provide only each year's slice, allowing control against both total project cost and each year's allotment.

q: The exponential smoothing method of forecasting sales differs from a simple moving average of past sales mainly in that:

options.A: It gives progressively smaller weights to the older observations and the largest weight to the most recent observation, whereas a simple moving average gives equal weight to every observation included in it
options.B: It uses no past sales figures at all
options.C: It can be applied only to the sales of seasonal products
options.D: It always produces a lower forecast than a moving average

e: Exponential smoothing gives progressively smaller weights to older observations and the largest weight to the most recent one, whereas a simple moving average gives equal weight to every observation included in it.

q: The distinction between the budget period and the control period in budgetary control is that:

options.A: The two terms mean exactly the same thing
options.B: The budget period is the whole period covered by the budget, such as a year, whereas the control period is the shorter sub-period, such as a month or a week, at the end of which the actual results are compared with the budget so that corrective action can be taken in time
options.C: The control period is always longer than the budget period
options.D: The budget period relates to the cash budget only, whereas the control period relates to the production budget only

e: The budget period is the whole period covered by the budget, such as a year; the control period is the shorter sub-period, such as a month or week, at whose end actuals are compared with the budget for timely corrective action.

q: The master budget of an enterprise shows a satisfactory budgeted profit for the year, but the cash budget forming a part of it shows a heavy and continuing cash deficit in several months. The correct conclusion to draw from this position is that:

options.A: The budgets are feasible as they stand, because profitability alone decides feasibility
options.B: The cash budget must be wrong, because a profitable budget can never show a cash deficit
options.C: The plans as framed are not financially feasible in that form, because profit is not the same thing as cash, and the budgets must be recast, by altering the scale or phasing of operations, the credit terms or the arrangements for finance, until the cash position also becomes workable
options.D: The enterprise should stop preparing a cash budget altogether

e: Profit is not cash, so a satisfactory budgeted profit with a continuing cash deficit means the plans are not financially feasible in that form. The budgets must be recast - scale, phasing, credit terms or finance - until the cash position is workable.

q: The selling and distribution overhead budget of an enterprise provides for fixed salaries of Rs 60,000, a commission of 3% of the sales value and packing and freight charges of Rs 5 per unit sold. The budgeted sales are 20,000 units at Rs 100 per unit, but the actual sales are 22,000 units at Rs 100 per unit. The flexed budget allowance for the selling and distribution overheads at the actual level of sales is:
e: Flexed allowance = fixed salaries 60,000 + commission 3% of actual sales (22,000 x 100 = 22,00,000, so 66,000) + packing and freight 5 x 22,000 = 1,10,000. Total = 60,000 + 66,000 + 1,10,000 = Rs 2,36,000.

q: The budgeted sales of an enterprise are 30,000 units. The opening stock of finished goods is 4,000 units and the closing stock is to be raised to 6,000 units. Each unit of the product requires 2 kg of a material. The opening stock of the material is 8,000 kg and the closing stock of the material is to be raised to 10,000 kg. The material is expected to cost Rs 25 per kg. The value provided in the materials purchase budget is:

An enterprise has an opening cash balance of Rs 20,000 in April. All its sales are on credit: the sales were Rs 3,00,000 in February, Rs 3,60,000 in March and are budgeted at Rs 4,00,000 in April, and the collections are 50% in the month following the sale and 50% in the second month following. Its purchases were Rs 2,00,000 in March and are budgeted at Rs 2,40,000 in April, and it pays 60% in the month of purchase and 40% in the following month. The wages of April are Rs 60,000 and the overheads Rs 40,000, both payable in April itself, and an instalment of Rs 50,000 for machinery is also payable in April. The cash position at the end of April will be:

options.A: A cash balance of Rs 26,000
options.B: An overdraft of Rs 16,000
options.C: A cash balance of Rs 36,000
options.D: An overdraft of Rs 24,000

e: Collections in April = 50% of March sales 3,60,000 + 50% of February sales 3,00,000 = 1,80,000 + 1,50,000 = Rs 3,30,000. Payments = purchases (60% of 2,40,000 + 40% of 2,00,000 = 2,24,000) + wages 60,000 + overheads 40,000 + machinery 50,000 = Rs 3,74,000. Closing = 20,000 + 3,30,000 - 3,74,000 = -Rs 24,000, an overdraft of Rs 24,000.

q: The credit sales of an enterprise were Rs 2,00,000 in March, Rs 2,50,000 in April and Rs 3,00,000 in May, and are budgeted at Rs 3,50,000 in June. Experience shows that the collections from credit sales follow the pattern: 20% in the month of sale, 40% in the next month, 30% in the second month following and 10% in the third month following. The cash to be collected from the debtors in June is:

An enterprise whose demand is highly seasonal follows a policy of producing at a level, uniform rate throughout the year in order to keep its plant and labour steadily employed. As compared with a policy of producing in step with the demand, this level production policy will generally mean that:

options.A: Finished goods accumulate during the slack season and are drawn down in the peak season, so that the average stock carried, and therefore the working capital locked up in finished goods, is higher
options.B: No stock of finished goods is ever held by the enterprise
options.C: The working capital requirement falls to nil in the slack season
options.D: The debtors of the enterprise are collected much faster

e: Level production keeps plant and labour steadily employed, but finished goods accumulate in the slack season and are drawn down in the peak season, so average stock and working capital locked in finished goods are higher than under demand-matched production.

q: An importer pays for his imports at the time of shipment under a letter of credit, and the goods then remain on the sea voyage and in clearance for a long period before they reach his godown and can be sold. The effect of this arrangement on his working capital is that:

options.A: His working capital requirement is reduced, because the goods are not in his godown
options.B: The goods in transit are not a part of his current assets at all
options.C: His funds remain blocked in the goods in transit from the date of payment until the goods are received and sold, which lengthens the period for which finance is needed and so increases the working capital he must arrange
options.D: The bank bears the whole cost of the goods until they are sold by him

e: Paying at shipment while goods are long in transit and clearance blocks the importer's funds in goods in transit from payment until receipt and sale, lengthening the financing period and increasing the working capital he must arrange.

q: The correct distinction between buyer's credit and supplier's credit in the financing of imports is that:

options.A: The two terms mean exactly the same thing
options.B: Under buyer's credit, the importer arranges a loan from an overseas bank or financial institution and pays the foreign supplier at once, the importer repaying the lender later, whereas under supplier's credit, the foreign supplier himself allows the importer to pay the price after an agreed period
options.C: Under buyer's credit, the supplier lends his own goods to the importer free of cost
options.D: Supplier's credit can be arranged only for the import of services and never for goods

e: Under buyer's credit the importer arranges a loan from an overseas bank or institution and pays the supplier at once, repaying the lender later; under supplier's credit the foreign supplier himself allows payment after an agreed period.

q: Under a trust receipt arrangement for financing imports, the position is that:

options.A: The bank keeps the imported goods locked in its own godown until the importer pays the full price
options.B: The importer acquires the ownership of the goods free of any obligation to the bank as soon as he signs the receipt
options.C: The goods are sold by the bank itself in the market on behalf of the importer
options.D: The bank releases the shipping documents and the goods to the importer against a trust receipt, the importer holding and selling the goods as a trustee for the bank and being bound to remit the sale proceeds to the bank in repayment of the advance

e: Under a trust receipt, the bank releases shipping documents and goods to the importer, who holds and sells them as trustee for the bank and must remit the sale proceeds to the bank in repayment of the advance.

q: On the TReDS platform for the financing of the receivables of micro, small and medium enterprises, the arrangement broadly is that:

options.A: The MSME suppliers upload their receivables arising from supplies made to corporates, Government departments and public sector units, and financiers bid to discount them, the MSME receiving the discounted amount and the buyer paying the financier on the due date
options.B: The Reserve Bank of India itself purchases all the receivables of the MSMEs at their face value
options.C: The MSMEs are required to deposit their receivables with the platform as a security for a term loan
options.D: The buyers discount the receivables of their own suppliers and pay them after one year in every case

e: On TReDS, MSME suppliers upload receivables from supplies to corporates, Government departments and PSUs, and financiers bid to discount them; the MSME receives the discounted amount and the buyer pays the financier on the due date.

q: Under a sweep facility attached by a bank to the current account of an enterprise, the arrangement is that:

options.A: The bank sweeps away the whole balance of the account at the end of every year as its charges
options.B: The enterprise is not allowed to issue any cheque while the facility is in force
options.C: Any balance above a fixed threshold is automatically transferred into interest-bearing term deposits, and money is automatically transferred back from those deposits into the account when the balance falls short for meeting the payments, so that idle funds earn a return without loss of liquidity
options.D: The deposits of the enterprise are transferred permanently to another bank

e: Under a sweep facility, balances above a fixed threshold are automatically transferred into interest-bearing term deposits and transferred back when the account falls short for payments, so idle funds earn a return without loss of liquidity.

q: The correct distinction between a pledge and a hypothecation of stocks for a bank advance for working capital is that:

options.A: The two terms mean exactly the same thing
options.B: In a pledge, the possession of the goods is delivered to the bank or its agent as security, the ownership remaining with the borrower, whereas in hypothecation the goods remain in the possession and ownership of the borrower and the bank has only a charge over them, with a right to take possession on default
options.C: In hypothecation, the possession of the goods passes to the bank, whereas in a pledge it remains with the borrower
options.D: A pledge can be created only over book debts, whereas hypothecation can be created only over cash

e: In a pledge, possession of the goods is delivered to the bank or its agent as security while ownership stays with the borrower; in hypothecation goods remain in the borrower's possession and ownership, the bank having only a charge with a right to take possession on default.

q: An enterprise is said to work with zero working capital when:

options.A: It has no current assets of any kind
options.B: Its current liabilities are nil
options.C: Its sales are made wholly for cash and its purchases wholly for cash
options.D: Its current assets are kept exactly equal to its current liabilities, so that its net working capital is nil, the operations being financed by keeping stocks and receivables to the minimum and by using the credit obtained to the full, a position which leaves no cushion and demands very tight day-to-day control

e: Zero working capital means current assets are kept exactly equal to current liabilities, so net working capital is nil - operations financed by minimising stocks and receivables and fully using credit obtained, leaving no cushion and demanding tight daily control.

q: When a bank which has discounted the bills of exchange of its customers itself rediscounts those bills with the Reserve Bank or a financial institution, the object of the rediscounting is that:

options.A: The bank obtains refinance against the bills it has already discounted, so that its funds are replenished and it can extend further bills finance to its customers
options.B: The customers of the bank get a second discount on the same bills
options.C: The bills are cancelled and cease to be payable by anyone
options.D: The liability of the drawers of the bills comes to an end at once

e: By rediscounting bills it has discounted, a bank obtains refinance against those bills, replenishing its funds so it can extend further bills finance to its customers.

q: A cash credit account of a borrower, as distinct from an overdraft allowed on his current account, is characterised by the fact that:

options.A: No security is ever taken for a cash credit advance
options.B: Interest is charged on the whole of the sanctioned limit in a cash credit account, whether drawn or not
options.C: In cash credit, a separate borrowing account is opened in the name of the borrower against the security of stocks and book debts, within the sanctioned limit and the drawing power, whereas an overdraft is a facility allowed to a customer to draw in excess of the balance standing in his existing current account up to a limit
options.D: A cash credit account can be used only for meeting the capital expenditure of the borrower

e: In cash credit, a separate borrowing account is opened in the borrower's name against security of stocks and book debts, within the sanctioned limit and drawing power; an overdraft instead lets a customer draw in excess of the balance in his existing current account up to a limit.

q: The annual consumption of raw materials of an enterprise is Rs 36,00,000, reckoning a year of 360 days. Because of unreliable supplies, the enterprise decides to increase the period for which raw materials are stocked from 40 days to 55 days. The additional working capital that will be locked up in the raw material stock is:
e: Daily material consumption = 36,00,000 / 360 = Rs 10,000. Additional stocking period = 55 - 40 = 15 days. Additional working capital locked up = 10,000 x 15 = Rs 1,50,000.

q: The annual credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 48,00,000 and the cost of the goods sold is 80% of the sales value. By stricter collection, the enterprise reduces its average collection period from 60 days to 45 days, reckoning a year of 360 days. The funds released by this reduction, the investment in debtors being reckoned at cost, are:
e: Debtors are reckoned at cost: cost of credit sales = 48,00,000 x 80% = Rs 38,40,000, or Rs 10,666.67 per day over 360 days. Collection period falls by 15 days, so funds released = 38,40,000 / 360 x 15 = Rs 1,60,000.

q: The total debtors account of an enterprise shows the following particulars for a year: balance at the commencement Rs 1,80,000; credit sales Rs 12,00,000; cash received from debtors Rs 10,50,000; bills receivable accepted by debtors Rs 1,20,000; discount allowed Rs 15,000; bad debts written off Rs 10,000; goods returned by customers Rs 25,000; and a bill of Rs 20,000, earlier accepted by a customer, was dishonoured and the amount was debited back to that customer. The balance of debtors at the end of the year is:
e: Closing debtors = 1,80,000 + 12,00,000 + 20,000 dishonoured bill debited back - 10,50,000 cash - 1,20,000 bills receivable - 15,000 discount - 10,000 bad debts - 25,000 returns = Rs 1,80,000.

q: The total creditors account of an enterprise shows the following particulars for a year: balance at the commencement Rs 90,000; balance at the end Rs 1,10,000; cash paid to creditors Rs 8,60,000; discount received Rs 12,000; bills payable accepted in favour of creditors Rs 80,000; and goods returned to suppliers Rs 18,000. The credit purchases of the year, being the balancing figure of the account, are:
e: Credit purchases are the balancing figure: closing 1,10,000 = opening 90,000 + purchases - 8,60,000 paid - 12,000 discount - 80,000 bills payable - 18,000 returns, so purchases = 1,10,000 - 90,000 + 8,60,000 + 12,000 + 80,000 + 18,000 = Rs 9,90,000.

q: An enterprise estimates its working capital as follows: annual consumption of raw materials Rs 12,00,000, stocked for 1 month; cost of production Rs 24,00,000, of which materials are Rs 12,00,000 and conversion costs (labour and overheads) Rs 12,00,000, the work-in-progress remaining in process for half a month, the materials being fully introduced at the start and the conversion costs being on an average 50% complete in the units in process; finished goods, valued at the cost of production, stocked for 1 month; credit sales Rs 30,00,000, the cost of the goods sold being 80% of the sales value and the debtors being collected after one and a half months, the debtors being reckoned at cost; and a cash balance of Rs 40,000. Its current liabilities are estimated at: creditors for materials Rs 1,00,000, being one month's purchases, purchases being equal to the consumption, and outstanding expenses Rs 35,000. A margin of 10% is to be added to the net working capital so arrived at, for contingencies. The working capital required is:
e: Current assets: raw material 12,00,000/12 = 1,00,000; work-in-progress = material 50,000 (half month, fully introduced) + conversion 25,000 (half month at 50%) = 75,000; finished goods 24,00,000/12 = 2,00,000; debtors at cost 30,00,000 x 80% x 1.5/12 = 3,00,000; cash 40,000 - total Rs 7,15,000. Less creditors 1,00,000 and outstanding expenses 35,000 gives net 5,80,000; plus 10% contingency = Rs 6,38,000.

q: In preparing the fund flow statement of a partnership firm, the interest allowed on the capitals of the partners and the salary payable to a partner are credited to the partners in the profit and loss appropriation account. In computing the funds from operations of the firm, these amounts are dealt with by:

options.A: Deducting them from the net profit, because they are payable to the partners in cash
options.B: Showing them as a separate source of funds in the fund flow statement
options.C: Adding them back to the reported profit, because they are appropriations of the profit of the firm and not charges incurred in earning it, the funds of the firm flowing out only when the partners actually withdraw money
options.D: Ignoring them, because a partnership firm prepares no fund flow statement

e: Interest on partners' capital and partner's salary credited through the appropriation account are appropriations of profit, not charges incurred in earning it. They are added back in computing funds from operations; funds flow out only when partners actually withdraw money.

q: Under the concept of funds as the total financial resources of an enterprise, as used in a statement of changes in financial position prepared on that basis, a transaction such as the issue of shares in exchange for machinery is dealt with by:

options.A: Reporting it both as a source of funds, the shares issued, and as an application of funds, the machinery acquired, because on this concept every change in the financial structure is reported, whether or not the working capital changes
options.B: Excluding it altogether, in the same way as under the working capital concept of funds
options.C: Reporting only the machinery as an application, the shares being ignored
options.D: Reporting it as an increase in the working capital of the enterprise

e: On the total financial resources concept, every change in financial structure is reported whether or not working capital changes. Shares issued for machinery are therefore shown both as a source, the shares issued, and as an application, the machinery acquired.

q: An enterprise holds forward exchange contracts purely for dealing and trading purposes and settles them in cash during the year. Under Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3), the cash flows arising on the settlement of such contracts are classified as cash flows from:

options.A: Investing activities, in every case
options.B: Operating activities, because the contracts are held for dealing or trading and are not hedges of any asset or liability
options.C: Financing activities, in every case
options.D: No activity, because a forward contract is not an asset of the enterprise

e: Forward exchange contracts held purely for dealing or trading, and not as hedges, give rise to operating cash flows under AS-3, because dealing and trading activities are operating in nature for such contracts.

q: A company receives a capital subsidy in cash from the Government towards the cost of the plant installed by it, the amount being credited to a capital reserve. In its fund flow statement, the amount received is shown as:

options.A: A part of the funds from operations of the year
options.B: An application of funds, because it relates to a fixed asset
options.C: No entry at all, because a subsidy is not earned by the enterprise
options.D: A source of funds, being a non-current receipt which has increased the funds of the enterprise without arising from its operations

e: A capital subsidy received in cash is a non-current receipt that increased the enterprise's funds without arising from operations. Credited to capital reserve, it is shown as a source of funds in the fund flow statement, not as funds from operations.

q: In an earlier year, an enterprise had provided depreciation on its plant in excess of what was required. The excess provision is now written back and credited to the profit and loss account of the current year. In computing the funds from operations of the current year, this amount is dealt with by:

options.A: Deducting it from the reported profit, because it is a non-fund and non-operating credit which has increased the profit without any inflow of funds during the year
options.B: Adding it to the reported profit, like the depreciation charged for the year
options.C: Showing it as a separate source of funds in the fund flow statement
options.D: Ignoring it, because a provision can never be written back

e: Excess depreciation written back is a non-fund, non-operating credit that raised current profit without any inflow of funds. It is deducted from reported profit in computing funds from operations of the current year.

q: The interest and dividends received by an enterprise on its long-term investments are credited in its profit and loss account. In preparing its fund flow statement, the correct treatment of these receipts is that:

options.A: They are allowed to remain as a part of the funds from operations, and nothing further is shown
options.B: They are deducted in computing the funds from operations and are then simply omitted from the statement
options.C: They are excluded from the funds from operations, being non-operating income, and are shown separately as a source of funds in the fund flow statement
options.D: They are shown as a reduction of the cost of the investments in the schedule of changes in working capital

e: Interest and dividends on long-term investments are non-operating income, so they are excluded from funds from operations and shown separately as a source of funds in the fund flow statement.

q: A manufacturing enterprise pays an advance to a contractor against the construction of a factory building for it, the advance being adjustable against the bills for the work as it progresses. In its fund flow statement, this payment is shown as:

options.A: A part of the current assets in the schedule of changes in working capital
options.B: An application of funds, because the advance is a capital advance employed in acquiring a non-current asset and is not a part of the working capital of the enterprise
options.C: A source of funds, because the contractor will do work in return for it
options.D: An operating expense to be deducted in computing the funds from operations only

e: An advance to a contractor for constructing a factory building is a capital advance employed in acquiring a non-current asset, not part of working capital. Its payment is therefore an application of funds.

q: A non-financial enterprise gives long-term housing loans to its senior employees, repayable over fifteen years. In its cash flow statement under Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3), the cash paid out on these loans is classified as a cash flow from:

options.A: Operating activities, because the borrowers are its own employees
options.B: Financing activities, because a loan is always a financing transaction
options.C: No activity, because loans to employees are a welfare measure
options.D: Investing activities, because for an enterprise whose business is not lending, the advancing of loans is an investment of its funds, the recoveries on such loans likewise being investing inflows

e: For a non-financial enterprise, advancing long-term loans - even to its own employees - is an investment of its funds, not its operating or financing activity. The outflow, and later recoveries, are investing cash flows under AS-3.

q: Some years after the forfeiture of its shares, a company reissues the forfeited shares and receives the amount due on them in cash. In its fund flow statement, the amount so received is shown as:

options.A: A source of funds, being a cash receipt on account of share capital, the forfeiture itself having caused no flow of funds when it took place
options.B: No entry at all, because the shares had once been forfeited
options.C: An application of funds, because shares have gone out of the company
options.D: A part of the funds from operations of the year of reissue

e: Forfeiture caused no flow of funds, but reissue of forfeited shares brings in cash on account of share capital. The amount received on reissue is therefore a source of funds in the year of reissue.

q: The net profit of an enterprise for a year is Rs 2,50,000, after charging depreciation of Rs 40,000, a loss of Rs 15,000 on the sale of its investments and discount on the issue of debentures written off of Rs 10,000, and after crediting dividends of Rs 25,000 received on its investments. The funds from operations of the enterprise are:
e: Funds from operations = 2,50,000 + depreciation 40,000 + loss on sale of investments 15,000 + discount on debentures written off 10,000 - dividends received 25,000 (non-operating income) = Rs 2,90,000.

q: The net profit before tax of an enterprise is Rs 4,00,000. During the year, depreciation of Rs 60,000 was charged, the provision for gratuity, which is treated as a non-current liability, increased by Rs 30,000 through the charge made in the profit and loss account, and a profit of Rs 20,000 on the sale of investments was credited. The stock increased by Rs 25,000, the bills receivable decreased by Rs 10,000 and the bills payable decreased by Rs 15,000. In a cash flow statement prepared by the indirect method, the cash generated from operating activities, before deducting the income-tax paid, is:
e: Operating profit before working capital changes = 4,00,000 + depreciation 60,000 + gratuity provision increase 30,000 - profit on sale of investments 20,000 = Rs 4,70,000. Working capital: stock increase -25,000, bills receivable decrease +10,000, bills payable decrease -15,000, giving cash generated = 4,70,000 - 25,000 + 10,000 - 15,000 = Rs 4,40,000 before tax paid.

q: The share capital account of a company shows a balance of Rs 8,00,000 at the commencement of a year and Rs 11,00,000 at the end of the year. Its securities premium account shows a balance of Rs 1,00,000 at the commencement and Rs 1,80,000 at the end. During the year, shares of the face value of Rs 1,00,000 were issued to a vendor in payment for machinery, at a premium of Rs 20,000, no cash being received on that issue. The cash received on the issue of shares during the year, to be shown as a source of funds in the fund flow statement, is:
e: Share capital rose by 3,00,000, but Rs 1,00,000 face value was issued to a vendor for machinery, so cash face value = Rs 2,00,000. Premium rose by 80,000, but Rs 20,000 related to the vendor issue, so cash premium = Rs 60,000. Cash received = 2,00,000 + 60,000 = Rs 2,60,000.

q: During a year, a company issues shares for cash for Rs 5,00,000, issues debentures of the face value of Rs 3,00,000 at a discount of 5%, redeems debentures of the face value of Rs 1,00,000 at a premium of 10% and pays dividends of Rs 1,50,000. In its cash flow statement under Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3), its net cash flow from financing activities is:

options.A: A net inflow of Rs 5,25,000
options.B: A net inflow of Rs 5,40,000
options.C: A net inflow of Rs 5,35,000
options.D: A net inflow of Rs 5,50,000

e: Financing flows = shares issued 5,00,000 + debentures issued at 5% discount (3,00,000 x 95% = 2,85,000) - debentures redeemed at 10% premium (1,00,000 x 110% = 1,10,000) - dividends paid 1,50,000 = net inflow of Rs 5,25,000.

q: During a year, the short-term marketable securities held by an enterprise increased by Rs 40,000, its accrued income decreased by Rs 10,000 and its prepaid expenses increased by Rs 15,000. Its income received in advance increased by Rs 12,000 and its bank overdraft decreased by Rs 30,000. As per the schedule of changes in working capital, the net change in its working capital during the year is:

options.A: An increase of Rs 33,000
options.B: An increase of Rs 63,000
options.C: An increase of Rs 87,000
options.D: An increase of Rs 3,000

e: Current assets change = securities +40,000 - accrued income fall 10,000 + prepaid increase 15,000 = +45,000. Current liabilities change = income in advance +12,000 - overdraft fall 30,000 = -18,000, which raises working capital by 18,000. Net change = 45,000 + 18,000 = an increase of Rs 63,000.

q: An enterprise has cash and cash equivalents of Rs 60,000 at the commencement of a year, which include a balance held in foreign currency. During the year, its net cash flow from operating activities is an inflow of Rs 1,10,000, from investing activities an outflow of Rs 1,50,000 and from financing activities an inflow of Rs 70,000, and the effect of the changes in exchange rates on the cash and cash equivalents held in foreign currency is a gain of Rs 5,000. Its cash and cash equivalents at the end of the year are:
e: Closing cash = opening 60,000 + operating inflow 1,10,000 - investing outflow 1,50,000 + financing inflow 70,000 + exchange rate gain 5,000 = Rs 95,000. The exchange effect on foreign currency cash is shown separately and added.

q: The first unit of a new assembly takes 100 labour hours and an 80% learning curve applies. The labour time required for units 9 to 16 (that is, the second batch of eight units) is:

options.A: 409.60 hours
options.B: 245.76 hours
options.C: 655.36 hours
options.D: 327.68 hours

e: On an 80 percent learning curve, cumulative time for 16 units is 100 x 16 x 0.4096 = 655.36 hours and for 8 units is 100 x 8 x 0.512 = 409.60 hours, so units 9 to 16 take 655.36 - 409.60 = 245.76 hours.

q: In lean production, 'jidoka' (autonomation) refers to:

options.A: Building quality in by giving machines and operators the authority to stop production when a defect is detected, so that defects are not passed on
options.B: Producing in very large batches so that set-up cost per unit is minimised
options.C: Keeping large buffer stocks between processes so that production never stops
options.D: Accepting orders only against firm customer schedules received in advance

e: Jidoka means building quality in at source: machines and operators are empowered to stop production when a defect is detected, so defects are investigated at once and are not passed to the next process.

q: A machine has a mean time between failures of 450 hours and a mean time to repair of 50 hours. Its inherent availability is:
e: Inherent availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR) = 450 / (450 + 50) = 450 / 500 = 90.00 percent.

q: Under material flow cost accounting (MFCA), the cost carried by 'negative products' (material losses such as scrap, waste and emissions) comprises:

options.A: Only the purchase cost of the material that is lost
options.B: Only the cost of disposing of the waste so produced
options.C: No cost at all, since a negative product has no sale value
options.D: The material cost together with a share of the system (processing) and energy costs incurred on that material up to the point of loss

e: Under MFCA, negative products (material losses) carry not only their material cost but also a share of the system (processing) and energy costs incurred on that material up to the point where the loss occurs.

q: During a month, 240 defects are found in the output of 40,000 units. Each unit has 6 opportunities for a defect. The defects per million opportunities (DPMO) are:
In set-up reduction (SMED), an 'internal' set-up activity is one which:

options.A: Is carried out by the factory's own employees rather than by an outside agency
options.B: Can be performed while the machine is still running on the previous job
options.C: Can be performed only while the machine is stopped
options.D: Relates to machines located inside the factory premises

e: In SMED, an internal set-up activity is one that can be performed only while the machine is stopped; set-up reduction works by converting internal activities into external ones done while the machine still runs.

q: The work content of an assembly is 54 minutes, divided among 6 workstations. The cycle time of the line is 12 minutes. The line balancing efficiency is:
e: Line balancing efficiency = total work content / (number of workstations x cycle time) x 100 = 54 / (6 x 12) x 100 = 54 / 72 x 100 = 75.00 percent.

q: Reliability-centred maintenance (RCM) decides the maintenance strategy for each item of plant primarily by considering:

options.A: The age of the item alone, older items being maintained more frequently
options.B: The consequences of each failure mode — for safety, the environment and operations — and whether a preventive task is technically worth doing
options.C: The original purchase cost of the item, costlier items being maintained more intensively
options.D: A uniform calendar interval applied alike to all items of plant

e: RCM selects the maintenance strategy for each item by analysing each failure mode and its consequences for safety, environment and operations, and applying a preventive task only where it is technically feasible and worth doing.

q: A product passes through three stages whose first-pass yields are 95%, 96% and 98% respectively. The rolled throughput yield of the whole process is:
e: Rolled throughput yield is the product of the stage first-pass yields: 0.95 x 0.96 x 0.98 = 0.8938, i.e. 89.38 percent of units pass all three stages without defect.

q: In materials requirement planning, the demand for components and sub-assemblies is described as 'dependent demand' because it:

options.A: Is derived from the production schedule for the parent products in which the components are used
options.B: Is forecast independently in the market for each component separately
options.C: Depends mainly on the production capacity of the suppliers
options.D: Fluctuates randomly and cannot be planned in advance

e: Demand for components is dependent demand because it is derived from, and calculated through the bill of materials from, the production schedule (master schedule) of the parent products in which they are used.

q: A factory's sales for a year are Rs 96,00,000. Its bought-in materials cost Rs 38,00,000 and bought-in services Rs 14,00,000. With 80 employees, the gross value added per employee is:
e: Gross value added = sales - bought-in materials - bought-in services = 96,00,000 - 38,00,000 - 14,00,000 = Rs 44,00,000; per employee = 44,00,000 / 80 = Rs 55,000.

q: In the lean classification of the seven wastes, overproduction is usually regarded as the most serious waste because it:

options.A: Necessarily uses the most expensive machines in the factory
options.B: Is the easiest of all the wastes to measure accurately
options.C: Can occur only in continuous-process industries
options.D: Creates and hides other wastes, such as excess inventory, waiting and unnecessary movement

e: Overproduction is the worst of the seven lean wastes because producing more or earlier than needed creates and hides other wastes - excess inventory, waiting, transport and movement - and ties up cash.

q: In the base year a shop produced 12,000 units in 3,000 man-hours. In the current year it produced 16,800 units in 3,500 man-hours. Taking the base year as 100, the labour productivity index for the current year is:
e: Base productivity = 12,000 / 3,000 = 4.0 units per man-hour; current = 16,800 / 3,500 = 4.8, so the index = 4.8 / 4.0 x 100 = 120.00.

q: Under condition-based (predictive) maintenance, the decision to take a machine up for maintenance is triggered by:

options.A: The expiry of a fixed calendar interval since the last maintenance
options.B: Monitored indicators of the machine's condition, such as vibration, temperature and oil analysis, crossing set limits
options.C: The breakdown of the machine in service
options.D: The availability of the maintenance crew on a slack day

e: Under condition-based maintenance, maintenance is triggered when monitored condition indicators such as vibration, temperature or oil analysis cross set limits, indicating deterioration, rather than at fixed intervals or on breakdown.

q: A bus depot's total operating cost for a month is Rs 16,20,000. Its buses run 1,80,000 km, of which 10% are dead kilometres run without passengers. The operating cost per effective (passenger-carrying) kilometre is:
e: Effective kilometres = 1,80,000 x 90 percent = 1,62,000 km, so operating cost per effective km = 16,20,000 / 1,62,000 = Rs 10.00.

q: In the DMAIC cycle of Six Sigma, the 'Analyse' phase is concerned mainly with:

options.A: Defining the project goals and the customer's requirements
options.B: Measuring the current performance of the process
options.C: Putting the improved process permanently under statistical control
options.D: Identifying and verifying, with data, the root causes of defects and variation

e: In DMAIC, the Analyse phase uses data to identify and verify the root causes of defects and variation, before solutions are developed in the Improve phase.

q: A captive power plant incurs a total generation cost of Rs 72,00,000 in generating 20,00,000 kWh. Auxiliary consumption within the plant is 10% of the generation. The cost per kWh of net power sent out is:
e: Net power sent out = 20,00,000 x 90 percent = 18,00,000 kWh after 10 percent auxiliary consumption, so cost per net kWh = 72,00,000 / 18,00,000 = Rs 4.00.

q: 'Heijunka' in lean production means:

options.A: Levelling the type and quantity of production over a period, so that work flows smoothly instead of in large uneven batches
options.B: Stopping the production line whenever a defect is detected
options.C: Producing each item in a separate dedicated manufacturing cell
options.D: Holding large finished-goods stocks to meet sudden demand

e: Heijunka is production levelling: the type and quantity of production are levelled over a period so work flows smoothly in small, even amounts instead of large uneven batches.

q: The manufacture of one unit of a product causes emissions of 0.04 tonne of CO2e. The enterprise applies an internal carbon price of Rs 1,500 per tonne of emissions. The carbon cost to be added to the cost of each unit is:
e: Carbon cost per unit = emissions per unit x internal carbon price = 0.04 tonne x Rs 1,500 per tonne = Rs 60.00.

q: In selecting a supplier on the basis of the total cost of ownership (TCO) of an item, the buyer takes into account:

options.A: Only the purchase price quoted by the supplier
options.B: The purchase price plus the cost of transporting the item
options.C: All costs over the item's life — acquisition, operating, maintenance and downtime costs and disposal, net of residual value
options.D: The purchase price less the discounts offered by the supplier

e: Total cost of ownership covers all life-cycle costs of an item - acquisition, operating, maintenance and downtime costs and disposal - net of residual value, not merely the purchase price.

q: A machine breaks down for 5 hours. Production is lost at 30 units per hour and the contribution is Rs 40 per unit. The repair bill is Rs 9,000. The total cost of the breakdown is:
e: Lost contribution = 5 hours x 30 units x Rs 40 = Rs 6,000; adding the repair bill of Rs 9,000 gives a total breakdown cost of Rs 15,000.

q: 'Tear-down' analysis, used in cost reduction, consists of:

options.A: Dismantling one's own product at the end of its life for disposal
options.B: Breaking down the total cost of a product into its fixed and variable parts
options.C: Dismantling a competitor's product to study its materials, parts and likely cost, and to find ideas for reducing one's own cost
options.D: Scrapping obsolete machines installed in the plant

e: Tear-down analysis is dismantling a competitor's product to study its materials, parts, design and likely cost, in order to find ideas for reducing the cost of one's own product.

q: A factory's electricity bill for a month consists of a maximum-demand charge of Rs 3,60,000 and an energy charge of Rs 4 per kWh on a consumption of 6,00,000 kWh. If the factory's output for the month is 2,30,000 units, the electricity cost per unit of output is:
e: Electricity cost = maximum-demand charge 3,60,000 + energy charge 4 x 6,00,000 = 3,60,000 + 24,00,000 = Rs 27,60,000; per unit = 27,60,000 / 2,30,000 = Rs 12.00.

q: Under 'open-book' costing in a buyer–supplier partnership:

options.A: The supplier discloses its cost structure to the buyer, and the two work together to reduce cost and share the benefit
options.B: The buyer publishes its cost accounts for all its suppliers to see
options.C: The costs of both parties are audited by an outside agency at the buyer's expense
options.D: Prices are fixed solely by reference to a published price index

e: Under open-book costing the supplier discloses its cost structure to the buyer and both parties work together to reduce cost and share the resulting benefit.

q: A company sells 50,000 units of an appliance. Experience shows that 5% of the units will need a warranty repair, at an average cost of Rs 180 per repair. The expected warranty cost to be provided for each unit sold is:
e: Expected warranty cost per unit sold = probability of repair x average repair cost = 5 percent x Rs 180 = Rs 9.00, which is the provision to make per unit.

q: Control limits on a control chart differ from specification limits in that control limits:

options.A: Are fixed by the customer in the purchase order
options.B: Are always wider than the specification limits
options.C: Apply to individual units, while specification limits apply only to samples
options.D: Are computed from the process's own variation and show what the process delivers consistently, whereas specification limits show what the customer requires

e: Control limits are computed from the process's own variation and show what the process consistently delivers, whereas specification limits are set by the customer and show what is required; the two must not be confused.

q: A buyer rates a vendor with weights of 50% for quality, 30% for delivery and 20% for price. The vendor scores 90 on quality, 80 on delivery and 70 on price (out of 100). The vendor's weighted rating is:
Taguchi's concept of 'robust design' aims at making a product or process:

options.A: Insensitive to the effect of noise factors, such as temperature, humidity and wear, which are difficult or costly to control
options.B: Physically stronger by using thicker and heavier materials
options.C: Capable of being produced only under controlled laboratory conditions
options.D: Free from the need for any inspection thereafter

e: Taguchi's robust design makes a product or process insensitive to noise factors such as temperature, humidity and wear that are difficult or costly to control, so performance stays consistent in real conditions.

q: Annual demand for a component is 36,000 units. It is produced in batches of 900 units and the set-up cost is Rs 750 per batch. The total set-up cost incurred in a year is:

options.A: Rs 750

e: Number of batches = 36,000 / 900 = 40, so total annual set-up cost = 40 x Rs 750 = Rs 30,000.

q: The Crawford (unit) learning-curve model differs from the Wright (cumulative average) model in that the Crawford model applies the learning percentage to:

options.A: The cumulative average time per unit
options.B: The total time taken for all units produced so far
options.C: The time taken by each successive individual unit
options.D: The cost of materials consumed per unit

e: The Crawford (unit) model applies the learning percentage to the time of each successive individual unit, whereas the Wright model applies it to the cumulative average time per unit.

q: A store orders a material in quantities of 1,200 units and also holds a safety stock of 300 units throughout the year. The carrying cost is Rs 8 per unit per year. The annual carrying cost of the material's inventory is:
e: Average inventory = cycle stock 1,200 / 2 + safety stock 300 = 600 + 300 = 900 units, so annual carrying cost = 900 x Rs 8 = Rs 7,200.

q: Parametric cost estimating determines the estimated cost of a new product or project by:

options.A: Adding up the estimated cost of every individual work element from the bottom
options.B: Asking a panel of experts to arrive at a consensus figure
options.C: Taking the cost of the most similar past product without any adjustment
options.D: Using a statistical relationship between cost and one or more physical or performance parameters, such as weight or capacity, derived from historical data

e: Parametric estimating uses a statistical relationship, derived from historical data, between cost and one or more physical or performance parameters such as weight or capacity to estimate a new product or project.

q: The estimated cost of a new product is Rs 1,000 per unit, made up of materials Rs 500, labour Rs 300 and overheads Rs 200. Value engineering proposals are expected to save 10% of the material cost and 5% of the labour cost, with no change in overheads. The revised estimated cost per unit is:

options.A: Rs 900
options.B: Rs 950
options.C: Rs 945
options.D: Rs 935

e: Revised cost = materials 500 - 10 percent (50) + labour 300 - 5 percent (15) + overheads 200 = 450 + 285 + 200 = Rs 935 per unit.

q: 'Postponement' as a supply-chain and costing strategy means:

options.A: Keeping products in a generic, unfinished form and delaying their final configuration or differentiation until a customer order is received
options.B: Postponing payment to suppliers for as long as possible
options.C: Delaying the launch of a new product until its costs fall
options.D: Deferring maintenance work to the next accounting period

e: Postponement keeps products in a generic, unfinished form and delays final configuration or differentiation until a customer order is received, reducing finished-goods variety and obsolescence risk.

q: In a process, 2,000 units are started. Of these, 1,760 units pass inspection the first time, 160 units pass after rework and 80 units are scrapped. The first-pass yield of the process is:
e: First-pass yield = units passing inspection the first time / units started = 1,760 / 2,000 x 100 = 88.00 percent; reworked units do not count as first-pass.

q: Deming described adjusting a process that is already in statistical control, in reaction to each individual deviation, as 'tampering'. Its effect is to:

options.A: Reduce the variation in the output
options.B: Bring the process mean exactly on to the target
options.C: Increase the variation in the output
options.D: Eliminate the need for control charts

e: Tampering - adjusting a process already in statistical control in reaction to each individual deviation - adds extra variation and so increases, rather than reduces, the variation in output.

q: During a year, 60 workers leave a factory and all of them are replaced. The cost of replacing each leaver — recruitment, training and lost productivity — is estimated at Rs 25,000. The average number of workers employed during the year is 1,500. The cost of labour turnover per worker employed is:

options.D: Rs 500

e: Total labour turnover cost = 60 leavers x Rs 25,000 = Rs 15,00,000; per worker employed = 15,00,000 / 1,500 = Rs 1,000.

q: The efficiency aspect of cost audit, as distinct from its propriety aspect, is concerned with examining whether:

options.A: Expenditure has been incurred after obtaining proper sanction
options.B: The plan of work was economical and the expenditure actually secured the optimum results that it was meant to secure
options.C: The cost records agree with the financial accounts
options.D: The stores balances agree with the physical stocks

e: The efficiency aspect of cost audit examines whether the plan of work was economical and whether the expenditure actually secured the optimum results it was meant to secure; propriety audit, by contrast, checks sanction and regularity.

q: For a component, the upper specification limit is 25.90 mm and the lower specification limit is 24.10 mm. The process standard deviation is 0.15 mm. The potential process capability index Cp, computed as (USL − LSL) ÷ 6 sigma, is:
An 'internal carbon price' used by an enterprise in costing and investment decisions is:

options.A: A tax actually collected by the Government on every tonne of emissions
options.B: A shadow price per tonne of carbon emissions, charged notionally to products and projects so that the cost of emissions enters the decisions
options.C: The market price of carbon credits bought from other firms
options.D: A provision made in the accounts for possible future pollution fines

e: An internal carbon price is a shadow (notional) price per tonne of emissions charged to products and projects so that emission costs enter costing and investment decisions, even though no tax is actually paid.

q: A plant consumes 9,00,000 kWh of electricity in a period, bought at Rs 7 per kWh, and produces 1,50,000 units of output. The electricity cost per unit of output is:
e: Total electricity cost = 9,00,000 kWh x Rs 7 = Rs 63,00,000; per unit of output = 63,00,000 / 1,50,000 = Rs 42.00.

q: Design for manufacture and assembly (DFMA) reduces the cost of a product mainly by:

options.A: Using cheaper grades of material for all parts of the product
options.B: Simplifying the design — reducing the number of parts and making the remaining parts easy to handle and assemble — at the design stage itself
options.C: Increasing the running speed of the assembly machines
options.D: Inspecting the assembled product more thoroughly

e: DFMA reduces cost at the design stage itself by simplifying the design - reducing the number of parts and making the remaining parts easy to handle, insert and assemble.

q: The total work content of a product on an assembly line is 84 minutes. Output is required at the rate of one unit every 12 minutes (the cycle time). The minimum number of workstations needed on the line is:
e: Minimum workstations = total work content / cycle time = 84 / 12 = 7 workstations.

q: Under extended producer responsibility, the end-of-life costs of a product, such as the cost of taking it back and recycling it, are treated in life-cycle costing as:

options.A: Part of the producer's own life-cycle cost of the product, to be provided for and reflected in product decisions
options.B: Costs of the customer alone, never of the producer
options.C: A general overhead of the year in which the product happens to be returned
options.D: Excluded from costing altogether, as they arise after the sale

e: Under extended producer responsibility, end-of-life take-back and recycling costs are part of the producer's own life-cycle cost of the product, to be provided for and reflected in product decisions.

q: In distribution costing, warehousing, order processing, packing, despatch and invoicing costs are classified as:

options.A: Order-getting costs
options.B: Product-sustaining costs
options.C: Order-filling costs
options.D: Facility-sustaining costs

e: Warehousing, order processing, packing, despatch and invoicing are order-filling costs in distribution costing - costs of fulfilling orders already obtained, as distinct from order-getting costs of selling.

q: The market price of a company's share is Rs 150. The dividend expected on it at the end of the coming year is Rs 7.50 per share and the shareholders require a return of 14% per annum. On the dividend growth model, price being equal to the expected dividend divided by the excess of the required return over the growth rate, the constant rate of growth of dividends implied by this price is:
e: By the dividend growth model, P = D1 / (Ke - g), so 150 = 7.50 / (0.14 - g), giving 0.14 - g = 7.50 / 150 = 0.05 and hence g = 9 percent.

q: For the current year, the board of an enterprise has itself fixed a ceiling of Rs 20 crore on the total capital expenditure that may be undertaken, although its bankers are willing to lend considerably more and several profitable works are available. The rationing of capital in this case is of the kind described as:

options.A: Soft capital rationing, because the limit is imposed by the management itself and not forced on it by the capital market
options.B: Hard capital rationing, because the capital market has refused to supply the funds
options.C: Capital rationing imposed by a statutory ceiling on borrowings
options.D: No rationing at all, because profitable works are available

e: Rationing imposed by a self-fixed management ceiling, when outside finance and profitable projects are available, is soft capital rationing; hard rationing is imposed by the capital market refusing funds.

q: An investor buys a share at Rs 250, receives a dividend of Rs 20 on it during the year and sells it at the end of the year at Rs 280. His total (holding period) return on the share for the year is:
e: Holding period return = (selling price - purchase price + dividend) / purchase price x 100 = (280 - 250 + 20) / 250 x 100 = 50 / 250 x 100 = 20 percent.

q: In capital budgeting, the two kinds of decision are commonly distinguished as screening decisions and preference decisions. A screening decision is one which:

options.A: Chooses between two projects that have both already been found acceptable
options.B: Ranks all the acceptable projects in the order of their profitability
options.C: Decides how the accepted projects are to be financed
options.D: Asks whether a proposed project meets a preset standard of acceptance, such as a positive net present value or a minimum rate of return

e: A screening decision asks whether a proposed project meets a preset standard of acceptance, such as a positive NPV or a minimum rate of return; choosing among projects already screened as acceptable is a preference decision.

q: The weighted average cost of capital of an enterprise works out to 10.6%. Its cost of equity capital is 16% and its after-tax cost of debt is 7%. The proportion of equity in the capital structure on which this weighted average rests is:
e: WACC = w x 16 + (1 - w) x 7 = 10.6, so 7 + 9w = 10.6, w = 3.6 / 9 = 0.40, i.e. equity forms 40 percent of the capital structure.
